speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We will make a number of moves this year to grow dispute resolution work in Singapore to the next level, and these amendments for the Civil Law (Amendment) Bill are one of those moves.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Compared to international commercial mediation, international commercial arbitration in Singapore is more developed.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: SIAC is now amongst the top five most preferred arbitral institutions in the world.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: It set a record in 2015 for the number of new cases and dispute quantum.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: I am confident that in 2016, SIAC would have done even better.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Singapore is now one of the top five most preferred seats in arbitration in the world, alongside London, Paris, Geneva and Hong Kong.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: But we are not resting on our laurels.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We will need to stay responsive to business and constantly adapt what we do to better serve their needs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: One area where we can do so is in third-party funding in international commercial arbitration, where legal costs can be substantial and where there is today a growing body of reputable professional funders.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: There are two main aspects to third-party funding.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: First, as the name suggests, third-party funding involves the funding of a claim by a party who is unconnected to the dispute.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The party, usually the claimant, uses the funds to cover its legal costs in the dispute.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Second, in return for the funds, the funder usually receives a share of the damages awarded if the claim succeeds.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: If the claim fails, the claimant does not have to repay the funder.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This is the risk that the funder takes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Maintenance is the provision of assistance to a party by a person or entity that has no interest in the proceedings.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Champerty is maintenance of an action in return for a share in the proceeds of the action.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: There are two aspects of champerty and maintenance.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: First, there is a common law tort of champerty and maintenance.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Second, also, under contract law, agreements affected by maintenance or champerty are void as contrary to public policy.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: These laws on champerty and maintenance were inherited from English common law.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: They were originally developed in medieval times to protect vulnerable litigants and to guard against potential abuse of court processes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: However, jurisdictions, such as the UK and parts of Australia, have decided that such protections are no longer necessary and have removed them.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Third-party funding of dispute resolution has emerged, driven on the demand-side by business needs for such financing options and on the supply-side by well-capitalised professional third-party funders.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: These third-party funders raise capital from investors and use the money to fund claims.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Their objective is to make an attractive return for their investors out of the proceeds of the claims that are successful.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Today, third-party funding has become a feature in other leading arbitration centres, including London, Paris and Geneva.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: As a leading centre for international commercial arbitration, Singapore is cognisant of the practices and business requirements of commercial parties, many of whom choose to arbitrate in Singapore, despite their dispute having no connection to Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: In this context, the Bill, which will introduce a framework for third-party funding in Singapore, will achieve the following outcomes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: (a) It will offer businesses an additional financing and risk management tool when engaged in the relevant categories of proceedings.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This includes the financing of valid claims which they may otherwise not pursue, due to financial constraints.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: (b) Businesses that seek to access third-party funding will typically have to undergo a rigorous process of claim assessment by the chosen funder.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: (c) Funders are known to be highly selective, given that they need to provide attractive returns to their investors.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Thus, their due diligence process is designed to provide them with a degree of confidence that the claims they fund will succeed.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: (d) Offering third-party funding, which is already available in other international arbitration centres, will strengthen Singapore's position as a premier international commercial dispute resolution hub and a key arbitration seat in the world.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This will benefit Singapore law firms and lawyers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: I will now take the House through the main features of the Bill.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The Bill provides a framework for third-party funding in Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The Bill does the following in relation to the laws of champerty and maintenance.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The Bill makes clear that while the tort is abolished, contracts affected by maintenance and champerty will continue to be contrary to public policy or, otherwise, illegal.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: These categories will be specified in subsidiary legislation after the Bill comes into force.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Drawing from the experience of other jurisdictions which permit third-party funding, there will be limited but targeted regulation of third-party funders.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The Bill provides that third-party funding may only be provided by an entity which meets the criteria set out in subsidiary legislation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The criteria in the subsidiary legislation will ensure that only professional funders whose principal business is funding claims, will be allowed.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The Bill also allows requirements to be imposed on funders through subsidiary legislation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Entities that do not meet the criteria to fund, or funders who do not comply with requirements imposed on them, will not be able to enforce their rights under a third-party funding agreement.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This would include their right to receive a share of damages, should the claim succeed.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The funder would, however, be required to continue performing its obligation under the third-party funding agreement, including its obligation to fund the claim, as the Bill provides that the rights of any other party against the funder under the third-party funding agreement are not affected.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: To ensure fairness to the funders, the Court or Arbitral Tribunal may grant relief to the funders on their application, if the non-compliance was due to inadvertence or some other sufficient cause, or if it is just and equitable to do so.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Disclosure of third-party funding is necessary to ensure there is no conflict of interest.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: It is anticipated that similar to other jurisdictions where third-party funding is prevalent, industry-promulgated guidelines or best practices will emerge.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: MinLaw is working with arbitration institutions and practitioners to initiate the production of such "soft laws".

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The Bill also makes a related amendment to the Legal Profession Act to clarify that lawyers are allowed to introduce or refer funders to their clients.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Lawyers are also allowed to advise or act for their clients in relation to the third-party funding contract.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: However, the Bill provides that lawyers are not allowed to receive direct financial benefit from the introduction or referral of the funder.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Direct financial benefit does not include legal fees paid to the lawyers for the provision of legal services.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Lawyers can be paid for the provision of legal services to the funded party.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Such payment can be made by the funded party or by the funder on behalf of the funded party.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The framework will facilitate the use of third-party funding in appropriate cases, commencing with international arbitration proceedings.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The amendments contemplated will level the playing field so that international businesses which arbitrate in Singapore are able to make use of the financing and risk management tools available to them in other major arbitration centres.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: At the same time, we will continue to monitor the third-party funding landscape here and abroad and will seek to ensure that best practices are adopted here.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: These companies treat arbitration or litigation claims as assets.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Like insurance, they distribute risks across their portfolio cases and, in the process, they are able to also invest in claims which are otherwise regarded to have lesser merits and may not otherwise see the light of day.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I recognise that third-party funding has been in existence in some jurisdictions for some time.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Third-party funding may be growing, but it is not without controversy.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In countries where third-party funding is allowed, the following problems have been raised.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If so, would this not be desirable because it would no longer be about the claimant's interests?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For example, the claimant may wish to conduct the claim proceedings in a certain manner or may wish to settle the claim at some point, but the third-party funders may disagree, and the third-party funders' preference will prevail if the third-party funding agreement ceded control and decision-making for the claim to the third-party funders.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Two, there is also the issue of conflicts of interest for the lawyers who are acting on behalf of the claimants in a claim funded by third-party funders.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Can the same lawyers act for both the claimants and the third-party funders without being in a position of conflict?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In many cases, lawyers or even arbitrators have been routinely appointed by the same third-party funders in different cases.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Clearly, in such cases, there is a huge question mark over whether the interests of the claimants are protected or compromised.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The claimants are left with no one to protect their interests if their position differs from that of the third-party funders, and I do not think this is desirable.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In the context of international arbitration, Chief Justice Sundaresh Menon said in 2013 that, "International arbitration features the unique situation of counsel and arbitrators often being drawn from essentially the same pool".

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Chief Justice also said, "A potential problem can arise when a funder finances multiple arbitral claims and where an arbitrator in one of those claims is also the legal representative of the claimant in a separate claim that is being financed by the same funder".

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Chief Justice also raised questions about third-party funders having influence over the arbitration proceedings and appointing arbitrators who have prior commercial relationships with the third-party funders.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: He asked whether such relationships should be disclosable to the other party.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In some reported cases, third-party funders have entered into third-party funding agreements with claimants which encourage claimants to settle a claim for more money by increasing the claimants' share of the recovered amount, if it is beyond a certain specified sum.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Claimants may, in such cases, reject what may otherwise be a fair settlement sum with their opponents earlier on in the proceedings, in the hopes of getting a higher recovery later on, but which may not ultimately prevail.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Four, third-party funders effectively become the new additional party to any proceedings which has an interest in the proceedings, which is to effect maximum returns on its investment, which may run in conflict with the interests of not just the claimants they are funding, but also to the prejudice of the defendants on the opposite side on how the claim should be conducted, and whether settlement should be entered into.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Will all these issues be addressed in the subsidiary legislation that the Senior Minister of State has mentioned?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Will this mean that third-party funders will be allowed to fund the setting up of a law firm's litigation department, which I read that such funders do in some jurisdictions?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If so, would there be a conflict of interest for lawyers vis-a-vis the third-party funders and the actual claimant?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Traditionally, in the past, this amounted to the tort and crime of champerty and maintenance.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: The Courts were also cautious in guarding against the abuse of the Court's process, fearing that a third-party funder "might be tempted, for his own personal gain, to inflame damages, to suppress evidence, or even to suborn witnesses".

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: But this position changed in the UK and the other common law jurisdictions over the years.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: The UK, through the Criminal Law Act of 1967, abolished the tort and crime of champerty, though the champertous agreements remain unenforceable for being contrary to public policy, or otherwise illegal in contract law.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Today, as the Senior Minister of State notes, third-party funding is increasingly used in international commercial arbitration, where costs are increasing and substantially.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: It is utilised in arbitrations in major arbitration centres around the world, including London, Paris and Geneva.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: What of Singapore then, which has been described as the fourth most preferred seat for arbitration?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: I welcome this proposal of having third-party funding.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: In Singapore, as the law currently stands, "champerty and/or unlawful maintenance will be struck down as being against public policy".

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: In 2007, Singapore's highest Court held that champerty applies to any procedure chosen for the resolution of a claim, including arbitration.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: As I understand the Bill, our Courts will continue to retain the discretion to inquire into the nature of third-party funding in order to determine whether the circumstances reveal an improper motive or a tendency to act in an unethical manner that would "sully the purity of justice".

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: By allowing third-party assistance, this will promote legal representation and facilitate access to justice in commercial and investment arbitration, which would otherwise be sacrificed.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Permit me though to ask the following questions of the Senior Minister of State.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: First, on the issue of balance, could I ask the Senior Minister of State: will the Ministry tell us more about the balance it intends to strike between this need for regulation on one hand, and the parties' autonomy and flexibility in future amendments on the other?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Particularly, what is the role that it sees arbitral tribunals and institutions playing as a check against abuse of process by third-party funders?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Second, will Singapore be following in the footsteps of the UK by having a regulatory or self-regulatory body, or perhaps Australia which seems to focus on the avoidance of a conflict of interest?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Will there be a periodic review of this approach that we take in consultation importantly with the users of third-party arbitration funding procedures?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Does the Ministry envision that it could include not only security for cost but also adverse cost orders?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Are there plans to provide further guidance as to the factors that ought to be taken into account in a cost order against a third-party funder?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Given the proposed disclosure requirements through possible amendments to the Legal Profession Act in due course, what does the Ministry have in mind to allay third-party funders' concerns that their identity and amount of funding will be unduly exposed?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: I say this as, in my research, I notice that this seems to be a concern for third-party funders.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: While I personally support transparency, could this disclosure or over-disclosure have a "chilling effect" on the willingness of third-party funders to come forward?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: The current criteria for qualifying as a third-party funder are focused on capital adequacy in the Bill.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Will other criteria, in addition to capital adequacy, such as having a minimum claim requirement, to help to ensure that funders assess the merits of each case carefully before agreeing to provide funding be put in place so that claims are not "farmed"?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Recently, persuasive arguments have been raised in support of third-party funding, especially given the high costs of international commercial arbitration.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It has been used in arbitration centres, such as London, Paris and Geneva.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I support this Bill on two main points.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I would suggest for the Ministry to take steps to ensure that the process and mechanisms to all these are adequately clear.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Thirdly, given the complexities of the third-party funding market, it is critical that parties fully understand the details involved.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For example, what are the various products available to them?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: What are the terms on which they are being offered?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: What is the impact on their control of the proceedings, and what are the consequences of recovery if there is a successful outcome?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In this regard, I would also suggest taking steps to ensure that in practical terms, lawyers and parties are equipped with knowledge of funded actions.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Lastly, parties will also need to take appropriate measures to maintain legal privilege and confidentiality.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This area of law is always subject to dispute.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The amendments aim to ensure that Singapore remains a premier international commercial dispute resolution hub.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: There is, equally, another important objective that we should look at.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Third-party funding allows commercial funders to enable a funded party to litigate what the funder perceives to be a legitimate case.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In this manner, third-party funding facilitates access to justice by enabling parties who may not have sufficient financial means to prosecute their genuine dispute to do so.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Whilst facilitation of access to justice may not be the main motivation of a commercial funder who is focused on making a return on his investment, as recently recognised by the UK Court of Appeal in November last year, it is nonetheless "true that the facilitation of access to justice is an incidental by-product of commercial funding".

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I take this opportunity to comment on and seek clarification on the following areas of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: First, I note that the wording of the new section 5A appears to be adopted from the UK provisions which also abolished the tort of maintenance and champerty under English law.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Also similar to the UK provision, section 5A(2) maintains the law on maintenance and champerty in the context of the enforceability of contracts as a matter of public policy.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: However, I wish to highlight that in the UK, the UK courts have allowed third-party funding contracts for both litigation and arbitrations.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In fact, the UK court in the same case that I had mentioned earlier recognised that third-party funding "is a feature of modern litigation".

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Given that the proposed section 5A is similar to the UK provision which allows third-party funding for both litigation and arbitration, could the Senior Minister of State please clarify why it could not be left to the Singapore Courts to determine what contracts can be enforced or what contracts may be contrary to public policy?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In this regard, I wish to further highlight that the Singapore High Court, in a 2015 case, has already demonstrated a willingness to uphold third-party funding arrangements for litigation in the specific area of corporate insolvency.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Second, if the objective of section 5A is to specifically allow third-party funding contracts in the context of international arbitration, would it not be more appropriate for the International Arbitration Act to be amended, instead of amending the Civil Law Act, which has a far wider scope?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This is, in fact, the approach being contemplated in Hong Kong, where the Hong Kong Law Reform Commission is considering amendments to the Hong Kong Arbitration Ordinance.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I also note that in 2011, the MinLaw had, in fact, consulted the general public on whether third-party funding should be allowed in international arbitration in the context of proposed amendments to the International Arbitration Act.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This is especially where After the Event (ATE) insurance is already available for both arbitration and litigation.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: ATE insurance provides coverage for legal costs, subject to an agreed limit of indemnity.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It is essentially a risk management tool that allows parties to limit their exposure to costs if they are unsuccessful.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Further, the policy considerations of third-party funding in the context of international arbitration to enhance Singapore as an international hub for commercial dispute resolution are also equally applicable to disputes litigated in the Singapore Courts, especially the Singapore International Commercial Court, which was designed to enable parties to avoid some of the problems often encountered in international arbitration and to encourage litigants to use Singapore as a hub to resolve transnational commercial disputes.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Additionally, allowing third-party funding in the context of litigation and domestic arbitration would also allow litigants to pursue their legitimate claims where they may not have been able to do so.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In the preliminary report on the review of civil litigation costs in the UK in 2009 commissioned by the UK judiciary, also known as the Jackson Report, it was reported that there was a range of third-party funders in the UK, which provided funding in respect of claims of minimum values ranging from £150,000 to £25 million.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The same situation could also happen in Singapore where certain third-party funders may choose to cater to a target group of litigants or a portfolio of small claims for commercial considerations.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The Jackson Report cited five reasons why third-party funding in civil litigation is beneficial and should be supported.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: First, third-party funding provides an additional means of funding litigation and, for some parties, the only means of funding litigation.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Second, although a successful claimant with third-party funding forgoes a percentage of his damages, it is better for him to recover a substantial part of his damages than to recover nothing at all.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: A key group of potential beneficiaries for third-party litigation funding are small and medium enterprises facing cash flow issues but who may have legitimate claims.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I accept that there could be reasons for excluding third-party litigation funding for certain types of claims where there may be greater potential for abuse, such as personal injury claims.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I propose that, in lieu, we should consider providing better assistance for these "sandwich class" litigants who do not qualify for legal aid, for example, by enhancing the Litigants in Person programme or the Primary Justice Project.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Thirdly and finally, I note that there has been an increasing concern over the extent of control third-party funders may exert over the dispute resolution proceedings.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In the UK, litigation funding contracts may still be struck down as being contrary to public policy if it confers disproportionate control of the claim upon the funder.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: After all, the common law rules against champerty were developed to protect vulnerable litigants and to guard against third-party interference in legal proceedings to protect the integrity of the judicial process.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The extent to which regulatory requirements apply may also be adjusted, depending on the value of the claims.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This may incentivise third-party funders to provide funding for smaller value claims, such as District Court claims, where they may not ordinarily do so.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Separately, I also note that the proposed new section 5B of the Bill provides that where a funder ceases to be a qualifying funder, the rights of the third-party funder under the funding contract are not enforceable but the Court or arbitral tribunal may grant relief if it is satisfied that the disqualification or non-compliance was accidental or due to some other sufficient cause.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Would the relevant Ministry not be in a better position to determine if the qualifications and requirements have been met?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In the UK, third-party funders are regulated by the Financial Conduct Authority in connection with their asset management activities and supervised by the Association of Litigation Funders (ALF), which is an independent body that has been charged by the UK Ministry of Justice with delivering self-regulation of litigation funding.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The Association also oversees and administers a complaints procedure in respect of third-party funders.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In Hong Kong, the Hong Kong Law Reform Commission is considering whether the development and supervision of the applicable ethical and financial standards should be conducted by a statutory body or a self-regulatory body.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Given the potential risks of third-party funding highlighted earlier, it may be preferable for third-party funders to be subject to some level of supervision, something that the hon Member, Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan, raised in his speech.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: As a matter of parity, I note that the local insurance broker of ATE insurance is regulated by the Monetary Authority of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The insurers themselves are regulated at their places of business.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The Hong Kong Law Reform Commission has highlighted some risks with third-party funding, including the risk of money laundering.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Would it not be better for a regulator to be vested with statutory oversight, with the degree and extent of regulatory control to be adjusted accordingly?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Without providing for a regulator and simultaneously providing for a light-touch approach right from the word "go" would run the risk of not providing adequate safeguards to protect the public's interest.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: To conclude, while further clarification and clarity on the ambit, extent of regulation and supervision of the activities of third-party funders in Singapore would be welcome, I support the Bill in principle.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: It had always been a part of the common law heritage that while litigation was necessary, it should not be encouraged.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: There were several rules that had developed over the ages in common law jurisdictions, including the tort of champerty, which says that a person with no interest in a lawsuit should not be funding that suit nor have a share in its returns, or the tort of maintenance, where a person interferes in a legal suit he has no interest in.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Along with these two rules, there was also an additional rule which the current legislation does not address, and that is a rule that prohibits lawyers from having a financial interest in the outcome of a suit.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: All these rules were designed to prevent frivolous claims, abuse of vulnerable litigants and, in the case of lawyers, it was also to ensure that their primary duties as officers of the Court would not be compromised by trying to advance their client's case at all costs.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: These rules were developed at a time when there was a need and, obviously, would have served its purpose as it has lasted for hundreds of years.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The reality though is that access to Courts and legal advice is expensive and getting more so.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In many situations, an individual or entity may have no ability to pay legal fees but may, nonetheless, have a valid claim.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: A classic example that people can relate to is personal injury.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: A person who suffers a serious personal injury may have a valid claim but may have no financial means to advance that claim, either to pay lawyers or to the Courts, and may end up recovering nothing.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: So, it was in order to facilitate access to justice that many other jurisdictions started relaxing these rules.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The United States (US), interestingly, started by relaxing the rule on contingency fees, meaning that lawyers were allowed to have an interest in the outcome of the litigation.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This meant that a party did not have to pay the lawyer's fees upfront but could give the lawyer a quantum of the proceeds from any claim they successfully get.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The UK was much slower to relax the rules on contingency fees but eventually did that.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The UK, however, was one of the leaders in pioneering third-party litigation funding.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: What this meant is that someone else who has no interest in the litigation could help to fund that litigation in exchange for a return of the proceeds.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Singapore has prided itself on being a leading financial and legal hub, and the strong rule of law in Singapore has helped to facilitate this reputation.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I think the speakers before me, including the Senior Minister of State, have pointed out that we are one of the top hubs for international arbitration.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: However, unlike jurisdictions, such as the UK, Australia and even the US, we have, until now, not permitted more creative fee arrangements that allow financing of claims.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: So, in our competition to be a hub for international arbitration, Singapore is sometimes at a disadvantage.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In international arbitration, for example, where Singapore firms take on international firms from other jurisdictions, the international firms' clients may have more creative funding arrangements, which means that they may likely have a greater ability to prosecute the claim.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Likewise, when a corporate client is deciding which lawyer or counsel to appoint, they may choose the jurisdiction of the lawyer based on their ability to fund their claim.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: So, for example, they may decide to go to a London law firm rather than a Singapore law firm if they were able to get third-party litigation funding in London.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: So, in that respect, I think this is an important change that helps to mitigate some of the disadvantages that Singapore lawyers may face when dealing with international competition in international arbitration.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: One of the reasons that third-party funding was allowed in many other jurisdictions was to facilitate access to justice.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: However, if we look at the example of jurisdictions, such as the UK, in fact, the parties that use third-party litigation funding are mostly sophisticated corporates.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: And, typically, the corporates will choose external funding for litigation not because they cannot afford fees but because they want to share their risks.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: After all, litigation is a high-risk venture and you have to pay the lawyers' fees upfront.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: So, if someone else would share that risk, then the corporates may well make a business decision and they may also be happy to share some of the gains.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Contingency fees, as some of my colleagues mentioned, have also got a bad reputation.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The US, while being a jurisdiction where parties are very proud of being able to access the court, also terrifies business owners because of the astronomical claims that sometimes come out, and its horrible reputation ‒ I guess Mr Murali mentioned it ‒ for personal injury claims.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: However, I do not think this risk will be as great in Singapore for two reasons.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: First of all, we do not have class action litigation as they do in the US.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Class action means that you do not even need a named plaintiff to commence the action.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: You just need to define a group of people.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: So, this allows lawyers to actually take on claims on behalf of very large groups of unnamed people.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Jury trials are where a lot of the largest personal injury awards are made, and that does not exist here.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: At many of our Meet-the-People Sessions, we meet litigants who may have either personal injury issues or, more likely, claims for divorce or other personal issues for which they may not qualify for financial assistance under the current Legal Aid schemes.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: They may have the means to pay, but I guess, like the bigger corporates, they, too, may, in fact, want someone to share their risks.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Many have even asked me if there are any lawyers that would be prepared to work and then get a share of the outcome, and I have had to tell them that that is not the way the legal profession works in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I agree with my friend Mr Murali's suggestion that they should also go towards domestic litigation and domestic arbitration because, in principle, they are the same thing.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I would even go further and say it should even go towards contingency fees because, ultimately, the concept is the same.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Of course, rules can be developed around these, and there are many other jurisdictions that have these arrangements to which we can look to for guidance.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I agree with the ambit of the proposed Bill and objective to allow international businesses to use funding tools available in other jurisdictions and promote Singapore's growth as a leading venue for international arbitration.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: As third-party funding is becoming a feature in major arbitration centres around the world, allowing third-party funding in Singapore for international arbitration will offer international businesses an additional financing option for international commercial arbitration in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: However, I would like to highlight two suggestions for the Ministry's consideration.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I submit that MinLaw or relevant industry accepted organisations should promulgate a set of guidelines that would help parties to navigate potential areas of concern, for example, conflicts of interest arising from third-party funding arrangements in relation to the tripartite relationship of third-party funder, solicitor and client, as parties should mitigate risks through formulation of a third-party funding contract which covers these areas of concern.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: One example would be to emphasise that the solicitor-client relationship take precedence in the tripartite relationship and, especially, as solicitors are allowed to introduce or refer a third-party funder to the client.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Some of these potential areas of conflict are addressed in the new sections 3(A)(b) and 3(A)(c) in the Legal Profession Act.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: However, they could be further expanded on in the guidelines to cover other situations where conflicts of interest may arise.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: For example, a major potential area of conflict is in relation to settlements.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: While both funders and funded litigants have broadly the same interest in maximising any settlement or damages award and they will share the proceeds of the litigation, they can find themselves in conflict over whether or not to settle.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: This conflict can best be dealt with by providing that any irreconcilable difference over settlement be referred to counsel in the proceedings for a binding expert opinion.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: In the same vein, conflicts of interest which are thought to be inherent in funded proceedings can be avoided or resolved by ensuring that the lawyers' fiduciary and professional duties to the litigants are given precedence over any duties or contractual obligations the lawyer may owe to the funder.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: A properly drafted funding agreement will do just that.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: One example would be that the disclosure of client's privileged information to third-party funder should be made on the agreement that the third-party funder is bound to maintain confidentiality of the privileged information shared.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Another example would be the disclosure of funding arrangements to parties in the arbitration and to the arbitrator.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: In the public consultation on this Bill, it was stated that amendments to the Legal Profession (Professional Conduct) Rules 2015 were envisaged.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: These related amendments were expected to draw reference from best practices and international standards reflected in the revised International Bar Association Guidelines on Conflict of Interest in International Arbitration (October 2014) which provides in General Standard 7 that funding arrangements ought to be disclosed to the arbitrator and parties to the arbitration.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Allowing third-party funding in international arbitration in Singapore may lead to third-party funding organisations to set up and operate in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: As the number of third-party funders increase in Singapore, it would be ideal to have the third-party funders come together to design a code of conduct to self-regulate their involvement in third-party funding arrangements.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Self-regulation provides greater transparency and raises standards of funding arrangements whilst not being overly restrictive on funding arrangements.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: For example, the ALF in England and Wales is an independent body that has been charged by the Ministry of Justice, through the Civil Justice Council, with delivering self-regulation of litigation funding in England and Wales.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The members of the association are governed by a code of conduct which sets out standards of practice and behaviour to be observed by funders in respect of funding the resolution of disputes within England and Wales.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Murali Pillai asked about the scope of the third-party funding framework.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Specifically, he asked if the amendments should be in the International Arbitration Act, rather than the Civil Law Act.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This is because we want to have the framework tested in a limited sphere, where those involved are typically well-advised, commercially sophisticated and better able to bear the reduction in damages.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: If the framework works well, as and when appropriate, the prescribed categories of proceedings may be expanded.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The Ministry will consult closely with the profession and stakeholders on this, as we have been doing.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, that is why the amendments are to the Civil Law Act rather than to the International Arbitration Act.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: As a side note, I should mention that ATE insurance is a different product from third-party funding.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: While it takes many forms with varying features, typically, for example in the UK, it is used where a party pays a premium to insure itself against the risk of having to pay the opposing counsel's fees.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: As such, the policy considerations may overlap, but it differs from third-party funding.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Vikram Nair also asked about the implications of the proposed third-party funding framework for contingency fees and whether this opens the way for contingency fees generally to enhance access to justice.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: As part of the review of the civil justice system, event-triggered fee arrangements, including contingency fee arrangements, will be studied.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The issue of regulation of third-party funding was also raised, in particular whether we should do more to regulate funders and how to balance between the need for regulation while preserving party autonomy and flexibility.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Other points raised include the protection of stakeholders' interests and how we plan to deal with the bad practices associated with third-party funding.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Singapore is an international dispute resolution hub and, as such, a large number of parties, counsel, arbitrators and funders are not and will not be within our jurisdiction.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: A heavy regulatory framework will, therefore, have little practical effect and our approach should be focused on what is practical and  effective, taking into account the nature of international arbitration.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We also considered recent developments in the third-party funding market for international arbitration.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: There is now a high level of awareness and acceptance of third-party funding.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Certain funders have established good reputations and have flourished.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Bad practices have come to light and, with greater awareness, advisers and reputable funders have developed measures to curtail such practices.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In the White & Case 2015 International Arbitration Survey conducted by Queen Mary University, 71% of the respondents indicated that third-party funding is an area which requires regulation.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The preference, however, was for soft-law regulation, for example, through the International Bar Association (IBA) guidelines or collective self-regulation through a code of conduct.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The survey also indicated that regulation of third-party funding should mainly focus on disclosure rather than on the creation of a prescriptive, substantive regime.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This would enable tribunals to handle potential issues on a more nuanced, case-by-case basis.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: From the experience of other jurisdictions, abuses typically arise from lack of transparency and conflicts of interest.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This approach will allow for the regulation to keep pace with the changes in the industry and this would address the point raised by Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: As mentioned earlier, amendments to the Legal Profession (Professional Conduct) Rules will be made to require legal practitioners to disclose if their client is receiving third-party funding, but not the commercial terms of the funding agreement.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This will enhance transparency and allow the tribunal to avoid potential conflicts of interest.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Also, with disclosure, parties are put on notice and can take steps to protect their own interests.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The reason the obligation is placed on the lawyer instead of the funded party is to ensure that the disclosure requirement has practical and real effect since parties and funders are often outside our jurisdiction.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The parties may be international so they may not be here, but the lawyers, when they come here, will be present in our jurisdiction.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: As for Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan's question about whether the disclosure requirement will affect the willingness of third-party funders to fund here, I am happy to share that disclosure received support from the majority of international professional funders who responded to our public consultation.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This will also help prevent situations of conflicts of interest.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The proposed approach to regulation would be in line with that in other jurisdictions.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In Australia, the focus has been on avoiding conflicts of interest, coupled with reasonable transparency.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In England, funders are regulated by the Financial Conduct Authority, but only in connection with their asset management activities, and not their conduct in relation to funding of proceedings.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Nonetheless, some funders choose to become voluntary members of the ALF in England and Wales and self-regulate by agreeing to abide by a voluntary code.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: As mentioned, we expect similar self-regulation through the issuance of best practices or guidelines for arbitrators, lawyers and funders and the Ministry is already working with stakeholders to address this need.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: These "soft-laws" will cover issues, including the solicitor-client relationship, costs, confidentiality, legal privilege, withdrawal of funding, essential terms to include in third-party funding agreements, as well as control of the dispute by funders, which a number of the Members have raised.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Lawyers must be mindful of their duty to act in the best interests of their clients, and industry promulgated best practices or guidelines will help to bolster the legislative framework and ensure that all stakeholders, including arbitral tribunals and institutions, are fully apprised of best practices and standards.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This should address the very valid concerns and suggestions raised by Mr Louis Ng, Mr Patrick Tay and Mr Dennis Tan.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Such criteria will be set out in subsidiary legislation.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In other words, they will not receive a share of the proceeds should the claim succeed.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This would be a practical and effective deterrent against non-compliance.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: These are matters best left to the parties and tribunals.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In practice, cost orders against funders may be difficult as they are not party to the arbitration agreement.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Feedback received during the public consultation process indicated that parties have sufficient levers, including seeking security for costs.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I will now address some of the queries raised by Mr Dennis Tan.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: His first concern was whether there would be a transfer of control of the proceedings to the funders from the claimant.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The overall philosophy to this is party autonomy.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, that is something that should be dealt with in the funding agreement.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The claimant and funder should both have their own representation.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, in that way, you would have a lawyer who is acting in the best interest of the claimant and they can negotiate the commercial terms of the funding agreement in the same way as many other commercial agreements are negotiated.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The nature of this kind of industry is that if one funder's terms are too onerous, there would be other funders available that the claimant can turn to.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, the market will find its own level.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: With regard to conflict of interest, Mr Dennis Tan asked what would happen if the lawyer found himself in a position of a conflict between the claimant and the funder.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Again, this is not different from other scenarios where you have different parties and the question of conflict arises.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Ideally, the claimant and the funder should have their own lawyers.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: If, for whatever reason, they start off with the same lawyer, which is probably not a good idea, but if they do, and if an issue crops up where it is quite clear that the claimant and the funder have different interests, then the lawyers should − as all lawyers in this scenario should do − either discharge themselves from acting for one, or for both parties.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: It is no different from a scenario where, let us say, you are acting for two defendants and, for some reason, the defendants' stories start to conflict.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The lawyers know that in that scenario, they either have to discharge themselves or act only for one defendant.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I think Mr Dennis Tan had one more question, which was on the meaning of "direct financial benefit" in new subsection 3A of section 107 of the Legal Profession Act.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In short, lawyers will continue to receive what they have always received, which is, their fees, disbursements and expenses.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: What they ought not to be getting is the financial benefit, for example, referral fees or a commission.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In the scenario which Mr Dennis Tan described, where a funder takes an interest in the lawyer's litigation department or acquires the department, first, you would have to get around all the provisions of the Legal Profession Act, which will be very difficult.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: But even if you could get around that, I think the essential question would be: is the lawyer put in a position where he is beholden to the funder and cannot carry out his duties to the claimant?

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This is the sort of test which lawyers have to face all the time when they are deciding conflicts of interest and the lawyers in third-party funding situations will have to apply those strict standards to themselves.
